title: The US military’s race to make fake blood
raw_text: Its call sign was Morphine 1-2. In February 2007, the hulking dual-­rotor casualty evacuation helicopter had just flown three wounded soldiers to a field hospital in Balad, north of Baghdad, when another call came: an emergency mission to fly through an insurgent-controlled area in broad daylight. Typically, helicopters would be in a spot like this only at night, and with all lights turned off. As it passed near the city of Karmah, in the eastern side of Al-Anbar province, an insurgent fired a portable missile launcher. The tail gunner, who likely saw the shot roaring in, yelled for the pilot to make an evasive move. But the missile had already locked on, and the ensuing blast started a fire on board. After the pilot battled the failing machine for 58 agonizing seconds, Morphine 1-2 plunged to the ground. All seven crew members were killed. Why was the helo there in daylight? “It was getting blood and bringing it back. It was [on] what we call a ‘blood run,’ and [it’s] the highest of priorities besides casualty evacuation,” explains Lieutenant Commander Robert Murray, a Navy officer and program manager at DARPA, the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency, who studied this incident as an intelligence officer. Today, a chronic shortage of blood in both the military and civilian worlds is fueling a race to develop synthetic alternatives. title: Redesigning source control at Anthropic
raw_text: Redesigning source control at Anthropic Interesting piece from Anthropic describing why and how they built their own custom alternative to Git, based on the dramatic increase in rate of changes to their code after the past six months. In May 2026, Anthropic averaged around 2,500 code changes merged per day; as of September, we merged over 30,000 per day. They included a chart showing those changes. I had Claude modify their chart ( code here ) to add markers for the public releases of each of their models in 2026: This shows public release dates, not the date when models became available for Anthropic's internal use. My guess is that the introduction of Fable/Mythos class models is a key factor in the increased coding velocity. "Antique" is their new code review system. The source control system is called Scion, and sounds to me like a reinvention of centralized source control along the lines of Subversion. They had some pretty extreme requirements: The history of our main branch alone is almost 100 GB, and a compressed working copy is over 25 GB. We perform on the order of 25 million code checkouts per day for CI, before counting developer environments, agent sandboxes, and research jobs. Fetched naively, that would be over 600 PB of git traffic per day. The new system was built by a team of seven people, and the migration from Git was completed in five months. raw_text: Direct to Full Text Report: The State of U.S. Academic Libraries: Findings From the ACRL 2025 Annual Survey 25 pages; PDF. From an ACRL Post: This report focuses on U.S. academic libraries in fiscal year 2025 (the 2024–25 academic year). With the sunset of the Integrated Postsecondary Education Data System (IPEDS) Academic Libraries component after FY 2024, ACRL’s annual survey is the only source of comprehensive, national data. The results are weighted and therefore representative of all U.S. academic libraries. Key findings include: Library Staff: The median total full-time equivalent (FTE) staff is 7.6, a slight decrease relative to 2024 even as the ratio of FTE students to staff has risen. Expenditures : Median total annual library expenditures are $470 thousand, excluding fringe benefits. Libraries spend $523 per student FTE, the same as in 2024, suggesting that when adjusted for inflation, libraries have less spending power in real terms. Collections and circulation: Academic libraries continue to focus on electronic resources, with 79.7% of total collection holdings and 98.2% of total circulation in digital format. Visits: The number of people entering academic libraries annually increased by about ten percent in 2025 relative to 2024, reaching a median of 53,250. Information Services: Library staff share expertise through interactions with users one-on-one and in groups. title: In Memoriam: Jan Ewout van der Putten
raw_text: Op 30 september 2026 overleed Jan Ewout van der Putten, 78 jaar oud. Als secretaris-directeur van eerst de Vereniging NBLC en later de Vereniging van Openbare Bibliotheken was hij bijna elf jaar nauw betrokken bij de ontwikkeling van het Nederlandse openbare bibliotheekwerk. Samenwerking en inhoudelijke vernieuwing stonden daarbij voor hem voorop. Tekst: Eimer Wieldraaijer Toen Van der Putten in februari 1999 aantrad bij de Vereniging NBLC, bracht hij een ruime bestuurlijke ervaring mee. Hij was tien jaar plaatsvervangend griffier van de Eerste Kamer geweest en vervolgens zes jaar wethouder voor D66 in Den Haag. Hij kende de politieke besluitvorming van binnenuit: een waardevolle achtergrond voor een sector waarin gemeenten, provincies en rijksoverheid ieder hun eigen verantwoordelijkheden en belangen hadden. Zijn directeurschap viel samen met een ingrijpende periode van bibliotheekvernieuwing. De vorming van basisbibliotheken, veranderende bestuurlijke verhoudingen en de ontwikkeling van digitale dienstverlening vroegen om richting en afstemming. Van der Putten behoorde tot de landelijke hoofdrolspelers in dat proces. Ook droeg hij bij aan een nieuwe structuur voor het blindenbibliotheekwerk en de verbinding daarvan met het reguliere openbare bibliotheekwerk. Toegankelijkheid kreeg zo een concrete organisatorische vertaling. Zijn werkterrein reikte bovendien verder dan Nederland. title: Quoting Geoffrey Huntley
raw_text: If the agent isn't using my diagnostics library, I could introspect and update AGENTS.md, but there's still a delta, and it'll drift. Instead, I write a pre-commit hook that checks the git diff for direct calls to observability modules that bypass my diagnostics module. Boom: fail the commit, inject a prompt telling the agent to use the diagnostics library. All of a sudden it's ten out of ten. — Geoffrey Huntley , nobody should type code by hand anymore. here's what's left. You can read more from the series here . Late last month, Anthropic released a report arguing that the model GLM-5.3 poses a major cyberattack risk. The report’s core concern is that the powerful new model, released in August by the Chinese company Z.ai, is freely available for anyone to download and modify. Anthropic’s assertion is only the latest move in a long-running debate about whether frontier AI models should be made open, like GLM-5.3, or should stay locked behind the doors of the frontier labs. These days, much of the debate about how to handle open models is playing out in public—and there’s a lot of money resting on its outcome. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, who has a lot to gain if people continue buying their own hardware to run open models, advocates enthusiastically for the United States to develop more of them, whereas Anthropic’s Dario Amodei, who runs a company that could be undermined by cheap, powerful models, advocates for a more cautious approach. But beneath all these commercial incentives, there is real substance to disagreements about open models. “I think a lot of the way you come down on the openness debate is influenced by how you come down on the AI debate,” says David Gray Widder, an assistant professor at the University of Texas at Austin School of Information. title: AI labs are buying data from dead startups to train their models
raw_text: When Keelan Miskell began winding down his crypto startup this year, he didn’t think its data was worth much: the users were anonymous, the company just a few years old. But he’s since turned the firm’s digital archives into real money. He’s netted roughly $25,000 for his code base and a still-pending amount (likely around $15,000) for the workspace data in Google, Notion, Figma, and Slack. “At least all that stuff we were doing for two and a half years is worth something to someone somewhere,” he says. The sale was brokered by a company called SimpleClosure, part of a new growth sector in tech: businesses catering to dying startups. Estimates from Carta and AngelList show shutdowns rising between 26% and 56% annually in recent years, and an end-of-life ecosystem—including coaches, “death doulas,” and firms that help handle the legal, tax, and operational headaches of going ­belly-up—has emerged. Now tech undertakers are selling the data remains to AI labs. SimpleClosure added data sales to its services in April. Its Asset Hub platform helps founders sell their code and workspace data—emails, chats, documents. Buyers include foundation AI labs, vendors that construct simulated workspaces for AI training, and mature tech companies building their own models. Asset Hub has handled over 150 deals and expects to return over $10 million to startups by the end of 2026. title: Hello Python 3.15, goodbye 3.10, and now I can use 3.11
raw_text: Python 3.15 is here ! Here's the essential What's new in Python 3.15 guide, this year curated by 3.14 and 3.15 release manager Hugo van Kemenade. As someone who builds open source software that works in every supported Python version, I get to say goodbye to Python 3.10 and start embracing features from Python 3.11. First, some highlights from Python 3.15. Explicit lazy imports I'm most excited about Explicit lazy imports from PEP 810 . These let you import modules like so: lazy import json lazy from pathlib import Path The module will then be imported the first time those symbols are used in the code that follows. My LLM CLI tool implements plugins. I had to recommend manual lazy imports in the plugin author documentation, because simply installing plugins that used heavy dependencies such as sentence_transformers could add multiple seconds to every invocation of the llm command. Lazy imports directly address this startup cost. Unpacking in comprehensions The new [*sublist for sublist in lists] unpacking syntax is neat. Here's an illustration lifted from the documentation : lists = [[ 1 , 2 ], [ 3 , 4 ], [ 5 ]] [ * L for L in lists ] # [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] # equivalent to [x for L in lists for x in L] sets = [{ 1 , 2 }, { 2 , 3 }, { 3 , 4 }] { * s for s in sets } # {1, 2, 3, 4} # equivalent to {x for s in sets for x in s} dicts = [{ 'a' : 1 }, { 'b' : 2 }, { 'a' : 3 }] { ** d for d in dicts } # {'a': 3, 'b': 2} # equivalent to {k: v for d in dicts for k,v in d.items()} PEP 798: U

title: Metropolitan Libraries Spotlight: How Nanhai Library Is Reconnecting Children with the Classics
raw_text: When a thousand-year-old novel has to compete with a 15-second video In Foshan, in the heart of the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area, Nanhai Library serves a district of more than 3.7 million people, where local families, migrant workers, students, and seniors intertwine in a fast-moving, diverse community. It is also a community facing a very contemporary problem: as short-form video quietly absorbs every spare moment of screen time, deep reading is being pushed to the margins, even when the content at stake is centuries old. Rather than treat this as a lost cause, the library decided to meet children where their attention already lives. In April 2026, it launched Classics 101: Mental Models for Kids, a program built specifically for 10- to 12-year-olds — the exact age when children move from picture-to-text bridge books into more demanding reading. Making the classics legible again The challenge was concrete and specific. More than 60% of students in the first sessions admitted their biggest frustration was simple: they could not remember who everyone was or how all the characters connected. The semi-archaic language, sprawling character webs, and unhurried pacing of China’s Four Great Classical Novels were never designed to compete with instant gratification. So Nanhai Library stopped asking children to memorize plots and started extracting something more useful: practical mental models drawn directly from the characters’ journeys. raw_text: Welcome to Import AI, a newsletter about AI research. Import AI runs on arXiv, cappuccinos, and feedback from readers. If you’d like to support this, please subscribe. Subscribe now New benchmark shows how AI models lack intuitive visual reasoning: …Humanity’s Sixth Sense highlights some shortcomings of current AI systems… AI startups Elorian and Scale AI have built and released Humanity’s Sixth Sense, a benchmark that “measures how a model interprets and reasons through information a visual scene implies but doesn’t explicitly show.” Some examples of the types of task in HSS are a picture of a bookcase and being asked whether it can fit more books, or a photo of horses pulling a plough and a question of whether the chains bear the plough’s drag weight. HSS contains 522 questions that cover 288 images and 234 short video clips (totalling 17.6 hours of video). The questions fall into four categories: Temporal & causal dynamics: “What happened before the scene, and what happens next.” Physical & spatial logic: “What fits, what’s in reach, and what someone else can see from where they are standing.” Social understanding : “Intent, attention, belonging.” Abstract & contextual inference : “The patterns and rules a scene implies.” Results: The human baseline for this is not perfect, but is very high, with people scoring aggregate pass@1 of 93.1, broken down across four categories: Image (94.1), video (91.9), time (97), and space (94.9). title: The Download: moon city problems and drone traffic controllers
raw_text: This is today’s edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology. Mars may be a hellhole, but the moon is not far behind The US and China are racing to build bases on the moon, with NASA hoping to establish a small lunar city by the end of the century. But the moon is a tremendously hostile place to set up camp. A sprawling lunar base must be safe for its inhabitants, protected from falling asteroids, endless cosmic radiation, razor-sharp lunar dust, and torturous temperature swings. It also must be somewhat self-sustaining. That will require autonomous robots, nuclear power, and a way to use the moon’s resources to keep the base operating. But the chief obstacle may be one of political will. Find out what stands in the way of a city on the moon . —Robin George Andrews This story is from the next issue of our print magazine. title: Forse Vlaamse besparingen treffen erfgoedbibliotheken, archieven en kwetsbare lezers hard
raw_text: De drastische besparingsplannen van de nieuwe Vlaamse regering slaan diepe wonden in de archief- en bibliotheeksector. Naast het nieuws dat landelijke erfgoedbibliotheken hun volledige structurele subsidies verliezen en archieven de helft moeten inleveren, luiden nu ook de informatieopleidingen en de sector voor passend lezen de noodklok. In twee brandbrieven waarschuwen de Arteveldehogeschool en Luisterpuntbibliotheek voor onomkeerbare schade aan het Vlaamse geheugen en de toegankelijkheid van informatie. Ook de VVBAD (Vlaamse Vereniging voor Bibliotheek, Archief & Documentatie ), Openbare Bibliotheek Brugge , Universiteitsbibliotheek Gent en Erfgoedbibliotheek Hendrik Conscience roepen op tot actie. Binnen het nieuwe begrotingsakkoord van minister van Cultuur Caroline Gennez moet de cultuur- en erfgoedsector vanaf 1 januari 2027 structureel 47 miljoen euro besparen. Voor de grote landelijke erfgoedbibliotheken – de Hendrik Conscience-erfgoedbibliotheek in Antwerpen, de Openbare Bibliotheek Brugge en de Gentse Boekentoren – betekent dit dat zij 100 procent van hun jaarlijkse Vlaamse subsidies kwijtspelen, een verlies van zo’n 1 miljoen euro. Erkende stadsarchieven en instellingen zoals het AMVB in Brussel zien hun middelen gehalveerd. De officiële aftrap vond plaats tijdens de opening van de Kinderb Kinderen die met plezier lezen, ontwikkelen niet alleen hun taalvaardigheid, maar vergroten ook hun kansen om mee te doen in de samenleving en nieuwe perspectieven te ontdekken. dBos+ is een verdiepende aanpak binnen het landelijke programma de Bibliotheek op school dat inmiddels op ruim 70 Haagse scholen van start is gegaan. Naast een actuele en aantrekkelijke schoolbibliotheek krijgen scholen extra ondersteuning van Bibliotheek Den Haag bij het versterken van hun leesbeleid, het vergroten van de leesmotivatie van leerlingen en het verder ontwikkelen van de leesvaardigheid. Lezen opent nieuwe werelden Tijdens de feestelijke opening stonden boeken en verhalen centraal. Leerlingen voerden het Kinderboekenweeklied uit en gaven met vertegenwoordigers van de school, Bibliotheek Den Haag en ABC Onderwijsadviseurs het officiële startsein voor de Kinderboekenweek en dBos+. title: includi herontwerpt centrale bibliotheek van Grand Rapids Public Library (GRPL) in Michigan
raw_text: (Meer foto’s onder aan het artikel) Samen met inwoners en medewerkers werkt includi aan de vernieuwing van de centrale bibliotheek van Grand Rapids Public Library in Michigan (VS). Zo ontstaat een uitnodigende bibliotheek die meegroeit met de stad. Het project richt zich op het vernieuwen van de historische entreehal, de jeugdafdelingen en de gemeenschappelijke ruimtes op de benedenverdieping. Deze ruimtes worden getransformeerd tot een hoogwaardige third place: een plek waar mensen graag samenkomen. Hiermee versterkt GRPL haar rol als ontmoetingsplek die inwoners verbindt, waar zij zich thuis voelen en trots op kunnen zijn. Het resultaat wordt een vernieuwde bibliotheek waar iedereen zich welkom voelt. Een plek om boeken te lenen, te studeren, activiteiten bij te wonen of rustig de krant te lezen, alleen of samen met anderen. Een bibliotheek waar mensen willen blijven “We zien bibliotheken als echte third places (derde plekken): laagdrempelige publieke plekken naast huis en werk waar mensen elkaar ontmoeten. Hun deuren staan wijd open en nodigen mensen uit om binnen te komen. Ze bieden het comfort en de sfeer waardoor mensen willen blijven. En ze geven mensen de kans om te groeien. Hoe een bibliotheek eruitziet doet ertoe, maar wat mensen er kunnen doen en beleven is nog belangrijker. We vinden het een eer om Grand Rapids Public Library te helpen haar ambitie als ontmoetingsplek voor de stad waar te maken en kijken uit naar de samenwerking,” vertelt Aat Vos, creatief directe

title: Learning by Doing: IFLA Futures Club #5
raw_text: The fifth edition of the IFLA Futures Club offered an opportunity to explore what it looks like to apply futures thinking in libraries, in reality. Erik Boekesteijn and Cathelijne Kuiters of the Dutch National Library (KB) joined us to talk about their experience of running a concerted initiative to make futures thinking a more central part of the institution’s work, both with a view to shaping a new policy plan, and building skills more broadly. This was not the first time that futures had been on the agenda at the KB. Already, a ‘Club Stof’ had brought together colleagues throughout the sector, keen to get to grips with ‘the uncomfortable uncertainty of the future’. But with awareness that we are in a time where pre-existing ideas and assumptions are being challenged – epistemic turbulence – the Library’s new leadership was ready to take this work up a gear. There was an awareness from the start that this work provided an opportunity to think more broadly. First of all, an initaitive like this in the KB is not just an internal exercise, but also has potential impacts across the wider library field. National libraries usually have a kind of leadership within their fields, but the Dutch one has a formal role in supporting the country’s network of national libraries. What it does has the possibility to feed into changes across every local authority in the country. Opname-apparaatje ontdekt in vergaderzaal OpenAI, medewerker opgepakt
raw_text: AI-ontwikkelaar OpenAI heeft opname-apparatuur ontdekt in een van de eigen kantoren. Het Amerikaanse bedrijf spreekt van een "geavanceerd opname-apparaat". Het was geplaatst in een vergaderzaal in San Francisco waar vaak bedrijfsgevoelige informatie wordt besproken. OpenAI deed de ontdekking eind september. Het apparaatje was gewikkeld in wc-papier en zat in de usb-poort van een televisie. Daar zat het toen waarschijnlijk al twee dagen, zegt de FBI, die het onderzoek naar de kwestie leidt. Al snel leidde het spoor naar een Saudische werknemer van OpenAI. Die was te zien op camerabeelden bij de vergaderzaal, waar hij officieel geen toegang toe had. Ook zou de man (35) in de dagen ervoor opdrachten aan een AI-chatbot hebben gegeven die te maken hadden met het maken en opslaan van geluidsopnames. Verder is op camerabeelden te zien hoe de man achter de bewuste televisie naar iets lijkt te zoeken. Het opname-apparaatje was toen al ontdekt en verwijderd. Jarenlange celstraf dreigt De Saudische man is op 9 oktober opgepakt. Hij kan tot vijf jaar cel en een boete van maximaal 250.000 dollar krijgen. OpenAI heeft hem meteen op straat gezet. Het bedrijf zegt op X geen aanwijzingen te hebben dat hij waardevolle informatie in handen heeft gekregen. FBI-baas Kash Patel ziet in de zaak het bewijs dat het beschermen van Amerikaanse AI essentieel is voor de nationale veiligheid en economische voorspoed van het land.
